dharana.rendering: Let one imagine one's own body (the 'city') burnt up by the fire of time (kālāgni) rising from the foot; at the end, one becomes a tranquil radiance.

dharana.rendering: If one meditates on the principles (tattvas) of one's own body, or of the world, subtle and ever subtler, as dissolving each into its source, then at the end the supreme Goddess (parā) is revealed.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the technique of fusion (vyāpti): the gross elements are contemplated as absorbed into the subtle elements, these into the ego-principle, that into intellect, that into prakṛti and so on until all is reabsorbed in Sadāśiva; then parā devī is revealed and everything appears as her expression. instruction: Let solidity dissolve into fluidity, fluidity into warmth, warmth into movement, movement into space, and space into awareness.

title: Thick Breath, Thin Breath, Entering the Heart

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 55: Freedom in the dream state (Y28 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: pīnāṃ ca durbalāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagocare | praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktaḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt ||
dharana.rendering: Having meditated on the breath-power as thick and as thin in the region of the dvādaśānta, and entering the heart while meditating, one becomes free and gains sovereign freedom. (In the reading of Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja: one gains freedom in dream.)
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates: gross prāṇaśakti made frail and subtle by yogic discipline (particularly prāṇāyāma) and meditated on in the dvādaśānta or the heart. He then gives Swami Lakshmanjoo's traditional reading: 'thick' means breathing in and out audibly, 'thin' means slowly; meditating so at the dvādaśānta and the heart while falling asleep, one gains freedom in dreams. Singh records that Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 15) reads suptaḥ svācchandyam āpnuyāt and Kṣemarāja (Spandanirṇaya) svapnasvātantryam āpnuyāt. Wallis: prāṇa thick in the heart, tenuous at the dvādaśānta, and 'freedom in one's dreams'.

instruction: Breathe a few soft audible breaths, let the breath grow thin, and rest attention in the heart.

method.text: Breathe a few soft, audible breaths with attention at the dvādaśānta. Let the breath become thin and slow by itself. Then let attention enter the heart and rest there; in the traditional reading, while falling asleep. No breath-holding and no forceful breathing.

breath.cue: A few soft, audible breaths, then let the breath become thin and slow on its own. Never strain or hold. Natural breath is always fine.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The breath-power at the dvādaśānta and in the heart, first coarse, then fine
attention.secondary: Entering the heart as the breath thins

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the breath travelling between two places, the dvādaśānta and the heart, sometimes full and audible, sometimes thin and slow.
points: the dvādaśānta (commentarial: in front of the nose or above the head)

dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate the whole of reality, step by step, in the form of the 'paths' (adhvan), beginning with the path of worlds, as resolving from gross into subtle and from subtle into supreme, until at the end the mind dissolves.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh explains the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) of Trika: on the side of word, phoneme (varṇa), mantra and word (pada); on the side of object, aspect (kalā), principle (tattva) and world (bhuvana). The practice is to imagine the gross pair (pada, bhuvana) dissolving into the subtle pair (mantra, tattva), that into the supreme pair (varṇa, kalā), and finally all into pure consciousness, step by step (kramaśaḥ), so that the individual mind dissolves. Singh contrasts it with verse 54 (Door 031), which leads only as far as the revealed Goddess.

instruction: Let the solid world and your words resolve, step by step, into subtler levels and finally into awareness.

method.text: Contemplate the world around you and the words you think in as the gross level. Rest when the mind dissolves.

dharana.rendering: O doe-eyed one, by the use of a trick (kuhana), great joy arises at once, and through it reality is revealed.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads kuhana as a magical performance: the spectator's ordinary mind is lifted into mute wonder and joy, free of thought-constructs, and in that moment the nature of Bhairava is revealed; any awe-inspiring scene works the same way. instruction: When something astonishes you, notice the instant thought stops and rest in it.

method.text: When something astonishes you (a magic trick, a sudden beautiful sight, an unexpected laugh), notice the instant when thinking stops and joy rises. Turn attention to that instant itself and rest in it as long as it lasts.

title: Merging with a Great Joy, Such as Meeting a Friend

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 71: The Joy of Meeting Friends (Y43 ~ C1)

dharana.rendering: When a great joy is attained, or on seeing a friend or relative after a long time, let one meditate on the joy that has arisen; absorbed in it, the mind becomes one with it.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: on such occasions one should lay hold of the source of the experience, the pure spiritual pulse (spanda), and meditate on it until the mind is steeped in it; because the experience vanishes quickly it should be seized as soon as it occurs. Wallis: meditate on that joy as it slowly disappears; let the mind dissolve into it.

instruction: When great joy arrives, turn from its cause to the joy itself and merge with it.

title: Gazing at Space Dappled with Light

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 76: Patterns of light (Y48 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: tejasā sūryadīpāder ākāśe śabalīkṛte | dṛṣṭir niveśyā tatraiva svātmarūpam prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: Let the gaze be placed on space made many-coloured by the light of the sun, a lamp and the like; right there one's own nature shines.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'and the like' includes the moon, whose light dapples the night sky; in such contemplation the yogī casts off the limitation of objective consciousness and experiences the infinity of consciousness. Wallis: a space 'dappled with the light of the sun or a lamp'.

instruction: Rest a soft gaze on a space patterned with light, without naming anything.

method.text: Find a space patterned by light, such as sunlight through leaves, lamplight on a wall, or moonlight. Rest the gaze softly in the play of light without naming anything. Blink normally.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 76 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A space patterned with light: sunlight through leaves, lamplight, moonlight
attention.secondary: Seeing itself, rather than the objects

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a patch of space patterned by light, where the gaze rests without picking out objects.
points: a patch of space lit and patterned by light (sunlight through leaves, lamplight, moonlight)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never look at the sun or any bright light source directly; look at the light where it falls. Blink freely. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Five Seals at the Moment of Seeing

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 77: Krama mudrās (Y49-53; B2, A2, C2, A2 & A4 respectively)
numbering_variants.wallis_grouping: Wallis counts the five mudrās of verse 77 as five yuktis (Y49–53).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: karaṅkiṇyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā | khecaryā dṛṣṭikāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: Through the seals (mudrā) called karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā and khecarī, at the moment of seeing, the supreme attainment shines forth.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh, following Lakshmanjoo, takes dṛṣṭikāla as 'at the time of practice' and describes each mudrā: karaṅkiṇī views the world as a mere skeleton and the body as dissolved in the highest space; krodhanā is a tense, tight disposition; bhairavī keeps the eyes fixed outward without blinking while attention turns inward; lelihānā 'tastes' the universe as one's own I-consciousness; khecarī has several forms, including turning the tongue back toward the palate, and in its highest form is remaining in Śiva-consciousness. Wallis notes that the Sanskrit commentaries are needed to understand the verse and counts the five mudrās as five yuktis (Y49–53).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

method.text: Classical method: five seals (karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā, khecarī), each described only in commentary, are practised at the moment of perception, and the supreme attainment shines forth.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. The physical forms of these seals (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) are not taught by this school. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. These seals are esoteric and commentary-dependent, and some forms (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) can strain the body. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

title: The Space in the Armpits

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 79: Space in the armpits (Y55 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdhakuñcitau | kakṣavyomni manaḥ kurvañ śamam āyāti tallayāt ||
dharana.rendering: Seated properly on a seat, with the arms half-bent, let one place the mind in the space of the armpits; absorbed in that, one comes to peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates the arms as 'in the form of an arch overhead' and the gaze as fixed in the armpits, and says the arrangement is meant to put the mind at ease. Wallis and Bäumer read only 'half-bending the arms' and 'the space (void) of the armpits'. This door follows the verse's own wording (arms half-bent) and records Singh's reading.

instruction: Sit with the arms half-bent and rest attention in the space under each arm.

method.text: Sit comfortably. Let the arms rest half-bent, for example with the hands resting on the thighs, so there is a little space under each arm. Place the mind in that space and let it settle there. Lower or rest the arms whenever they tire.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition, with one exception that belongs to the verse: verse 79 itself says to sit properly with the arms half-bent; that arm position belongs to the verse, not to the school. That position is recorded in the method as part of the classical description, without any posture name. Everything else about the seat is a convenience, not part of the technique.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.secondary: The peace that comes as the mind settles there

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is two small hollows of space, one under each arm, where the mind rests. The half-bent arms only make room for them.
points: the space under the left arm
the space under the right arm

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the arms or shoulders tire, rest the hands on the thighs or lower the arms completely; there is no position to hold. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
